text: You'd think boolean would be the simplest data type in this whole course. It's actually one of the most inconsistent. Let's look at how SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL each handle true and false.
SQL Server has no true boolean column type. The idiom is bit, storing zero, one, or null. That column IS your boolean, in practice, even though the type's name says nothing about true or false.

Oracle is the most striking case here. Traditionally, there was no boolean column type at all for table storage. Developers reach for one of two conventions instead: char one storing Y or N, or number one storing zero or one. PL slash SQL has a boolean type, but only inside procedural code, never traditionally for a table column.

MySQL lets you write boolean, or bool, but it's not a real distinct type -- it's purely an alias for tinyint one. Check the column's actual type in MySQL's metadata and you'll see tinyint, not boolean.

PostgreSQL is the one real exception in this lesson. It has a genuine native boolean type, with true, false, and null values enforced directly by the type system -- you can even filter on it directly, without comparing it to anything.
Next lesson: auto-incrementing keys, where identity, sequence, auto_increment, and serial all solve the same problem in four different ways. See you there.
